Lost adolescence in Kallmann syndrome. I think it might actually be a strange paradox in my own personal experience of dealing with Kallmann syndrome is that my teenage years and early 20's were totally fine at the time. I might even say they were the best times of my life. It is only with hindsight that I realised I missed out on so much with missing a true adolescence and sexual awaking that I realised how much different my life should have been back then and how much it still affects me now. I can still remember being interested in looking at other guys when I when I was younger but at the time it was pure curiousity as to what I was missing out on not going through puberty, I had no other thoughts at the time. I can not remember the point when I eventually realised there might be another reason I was interested in looking. I am sure life is totally different for teenagers now with the internet and social media. As a teenager I was just patiently waiting for something to happen but I was not unhappy at the time. I should have started a lot earlier than I did and that experience would probably have made life easier now in terms of physical and emotional relationships.

Kallmann syndrome / CHH study & UK meeting - Puberty induction for young males and fertility treatments. There are two studies ongoing in the UK at the moment. One is a clinical study that is looking at the best treatment for young males with Kallmann syndrome / CHH to see if there are advantages or disadvantages between standard testosterone therapy and gonadotropin therapy in younger male patients. The study is a long term one and has only just started actively recruiting patients within the UK. The other study is a multi centre international review of fertility treatment protocols at different clinics around the world to try to identify the best fertility treatment protocol for male Kallmann syndrome / CHH patients. There is a patient meeting planned in the UK on Thurs 29th Jan to give more information on these studies with KS specialists from the UK available to answer questions and outline what the studies hope to achieve.

Kallmann syndrome is not the same thing as "delayed puberty". One of the major frustrations I have when telling people about Kallmann syndrome / hypogonadotropic hypogonadism is that they are not the same condition as delayed puberty. The majority of people with self limiting delayed puberty will have a totally normal, natural puberty and will not require any additional treatment and will normally be fertile. Howewever in Kallmann syndrome and similar conditions affecting the hypothalamus there is no normal puberty. Hormone replacement therapy can help with the symptoms but can not initiate or restore fertility. We require life long treatment. I get the feeling that sometimes when people hear about our condition they just think we were "late" and everything is ok now, somehow ignoring the fact we normally have to take hormones for life.

Genetics of Kallmann syndrome / congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism. There are two topics when talking or writing about Kallmann syndrome / CHH that can cause the most problems or are most mis-understood. The first is Kallmann syndrome / CHH is not the same as delayed puberty. The second is the genetics of Kallmann syndrome / CHH. There are very few clear cut answers when it comes to the genetics of KS. Unlike some chromosomal conditions the genetic testing for Kallmann syndrome / CHH is complex and rarely gives a clear yes or no answer. Current there are over 60 different genes, each with many different variants that have been associated with causing cases of KS / CHH. No one genetic test can possibly cover all these. Over 40% of cases still have an unknown genetic cause. The diagram belows shows some of the more common genes known to cause KS / CHH but there are many more. The one important gene is KAL1 (or ANOS1). This was the first discovered and the most pathogenic or disease causing of the genes. Apart for KAL-1, it can take two or more genes working together to cause a case of KS / CHH, which is one reason why it is so rare. KS / CHH shows every form of genetic inheritance. Inheriting a known genetic variant does not mean a person will develop the condition (penetrance) Other factors will affect how genes work in a person. Two siblings can inherit the same gene variant and have different symptoms or no symptoms at all (epigenetics).

IHH Progress: 3 months on hCG (Epifassi) + rFSH (Gonapure). Starting with zero sperm/small volume—anyone have success stories? Hey everyone, I (early 20s) was diagnosed with Isolated Hypogonadotropic Hypogonadism (IHH). I’m writing this to share my stats and hopefully hear from others who started where I am and successfully had children. My Baseline (The "Before"): Hormones: Extremely low FSH (0.15), LH (<0.1), and Total Testosterone (0.16–0.20 { ng/ml}). Sperm Count: Azoospermia (0 sperm). Testicular Volume: Started very small, around 1.5 { cm} 3. Labs: High AMH (>23), which my doctor says means my "factory" is just immature/dormant, not broken. Imaging: Normal Pituitary MRI (no tumors) and normal EEG. Medical History: Had a brief history of epilepsy in 2019 (seizures triggered by stress), but I'm off Trileptal now and have been cleared by my neurologist. The Treatment Plan: My urologist put me on: Epifassi 5000 IU (hCG) Gonapure 150 (rFSH) 3-Month Progress Update: I’ve been on this protocol for 3 months now and the "second puberty" is hitting hard: Physical: I have way more energy and I’ve started lifting weights. I’m seeing muscle growth. Libido: My drive is through the roof—almost hard to manage sometimes. Growth: My most recent ultrasound (Nov 2024) showed my testicles have grown from 1.5 { cm} 3 to about 6.5 { cm} 3. Sperm Count: My last analysis (at the start of treatment) was still zero, which I know is normal because it takes 90 days to make sperm. My Questions: For those who started with very small testicular volume (under 2 { cm} 3) and zero sperm, how long did it take for you to see numbers on a semen analysis? Has anyone with this "pre-pubertal" baseline gone on to have children naturally, or did you have to use IVF/ICSI? Did the "needy" high-libido feeling eventually level out once your body got used to the testosterone? It’s been a long journey from being diagnosed in 2019 to finally getting the right treatment in 2024, so any encouragement or similar stories would mean a lot. TL;DR: Diagnosed with IHH, started with 0 sperm and 1.5 { cm} 3 volume. 3 months into hCG/FSH, volume is up to 6.5 { cm} 3. Looking for fertility success stories.

Hypogonadism - physical and emotional effects. For any person the experience of having hypogonadism can be stressful, both for the physical and emotional effects it can bring to both males and females. While testosterone / oestrogen are not vital hormones for living they can have a strong impact on the quality of life. It is worse for Kallmann syndrome / CHH patients as we have to cope with the effects of physical underdevelopment as well as the effects of low hormone levels if we are not on the correct treatment. Treating KS / CHH is not just a case of replacing the hormones, all though this is a very good start. There has to be a psychological understanding to the condition as well. Some of the fellow patients I talk to have a good mental attitude to having this condition and can have a positive outlook once on treatment. I vary in my outlook, I try not be negative but it can be difficult sometimes. I do think sometimes that the patients who find the right partner at the right time can have a better outlook but even then it is a difficult condition to escape from totally. I think being able to talk about the condition helps, either to professionals or to fellow patients. I have been fortunate to meet a lot of fellow patients over the years, either on line or in person, which I think has helped me in my own journey with this condition.

Meeting / talking with other people with Kallmann syndrome / CHH. How many people have met another patient with Kallmann syndrome in person ? Do you think interacting with other people with the same condition can be beneficial. I met my first fellow patient in person about a year after diagnosis and then had a in person patient meeting about 3 years after that. Over the subsequent years I have met and talked to countless of other patients. I actually have no idea how many patients I have met in person but it might be but it has to be well over 100. I think with a rare condition such as Kallmann syndrome there can be a benefit in knowing that you are not the only person out there with the condition. For some people just knowing that they are not alone with the condition and there are other patients out there is enough and they do have the need to interact with other patients. I personally like the interaction I have, either in just helping with general information about KS or talking about totally different things. Since KS / CHH is such a hidden condition with an intimate part to it, being able to talk about it to somebody else, either a fellow patient or a health professional can help in most cases.

Husbands HT success after 1 yr. My husband (37m) has KS. For the last year and a bit he’s been on Gonal F and Ovidrel. This got him producing sperm but had nothing in the semen when samples were done but they were able to extract via a MicroTESE and the doctor told us he had Non-obstructive Azoospermia. Afterwards we continued on a normal dose of Ovidrel 6 clicks and 150 Gonal f but as the sample continued to show no sperm, he specialist trialed him on 3000iu of Brevactid for about 3 months now and he finally has sperm in his samples! We were expecting him to be on the treatment for at least 6 months before we had a successful sample!

How rare is Kallmann syndrome / congenital hypogonadotropic hypogonadism ? I attended three different presentations today that mentioned Kallmann syndrome / CHH and all three gave different values for the incidence of the condition. There is no doubt it is a rare condition, whatever defintion of the term "rare" you use. Estimates can vary from 1 in 10,000 to 1 in 100,000 depending on what source you use and if you are talking about KS on its own or all hypogonadotropic hypogonadism cases. A recent Finnish study put the figure at 1 in 48,000 and most published papers seem to go with that figure. I used to use the figure to try to estimate how many people had our condition in each country. The other way to look at it is to estimate how many people (approx) are born each year in a particular country. For the UK for example, taking the 1 in 48,000 figure and an annual births figure of 600,000, that gives a figure of 12.5 new cases every year. Certainly less than 20 people born each year with KS / CHH in the UK. Certainly in the rare category.

Kallmann syndrome - one of over 6,000+ recognised rare disorders. Over 6,000 recognised rare diseases around the world. Over 300 million people world wide have a rare disease. 70% of rare diseases are genetic in orgin and of these 70% start in childhood. Kallmann syndrome is often not easy to diagnose, especially in females. There is no one genetic test for Kallmann syndrome. Diagnosis is often made by exclusion of other conditions. Hormone replacement therapy and fertility treatments are available which can be effective in treating most of the physical symptoms. However the psycholological symptoms in missing puberty and adolescence are often not recognised or treated and can have a profound effect in some patients.

Experience of growing up with Kallmann syndrome / CHH. Differences between younger and older patients. I had a 2 hour interview with a clinical psychologist today. I found it an interesting and useful experience. It was a chance to talk about my experiences growing up with KS, my late diagnosis and my experiences with relationships. It was useful to talk to somebody neutral who had experience of talking to rare disease patients but wanted to know more about KS. It is something I think that would be helpful for all KS patients to have the experience of doing. One area of interest is whether there is a difference in experience through different generations. I was diagnosed and treated just before the internet and social media took off. My experience must be totally different to an 18 year old being diagnosed today. As a patient advocate I am happy to talk about my experiences with the condition but they are my own experiences and they will not be typical for other KS patients. I love to be able to raise the awareness of the condition but it is good to hear from as many people as possible in how they cope with the living with the condition. One period of my life I could not explain was the transition from childhood to adulthood, which was certainly not typical. I went from being a totally normal child to be socially isolated. It was my own decision but I can not remember ever making an active decision to exclude myself from social activities. I kept on making excuses not to be social so people stopped asking me. Perhaps this was one of the biggest mistakes I made with my KS experience.

Being a 20 year old "late bloomer". I am over 50, I really should not be writting posts about puberty. It is not through choice though, I really wish I had the normal puberty that the majority of other people go through I have no sense of smell and poor hearing. This was noticed in childhood but it was not really a major issue at the time. My childhood was just a normal, regular one. Then something happened, or to be more accurate something did not happen. Puberty. It is difficult for me to think back that far but I do remember thinking when would it start. I knew the basics but this was the pre-internet age so access to information on development was not really available. I can not even remember ever having any sex ed lessons at school. At 14 or 15, I had a medical with the school nurse. Not really sure why but I think it was for a permit from the council to be able to do a paper round (that does sound odd now I think about it). I was sent to my local GP. I can not remember the appointment but I must have been told I was just a "late bloomer" and should just wait and see. I had similar appointments at 16 and 17 with the same result. Just wait and see. At 18, I was sent to the local hospital to be seen by a general medicine consultant and an urologist. I remember the examination by the urologist who asked a lot of questions that a normal 18 year old would be able to answer but I did not really know what he was talking about. I can not remember any doctor noticing or remarking on the fact I had no sense of smell or poor hearing. After this I was put on Sustanon. I think it must have been 100 mg/ml and monthly. The dose was so low and so infrequent it made no difference at all. I went to Uni soon after and stopped taking it because it was doing nothing for me. I had to wait until I was 23, when working my first real job after Uni to get the correct diagnosis and treatment. That is another story.

Kallmann syndrome and relationships. I am not a good example of how to handle relationships (both emotional or physical) while having Kallmann syndrome. I have met and talked to plenty of KS friends who have been successful in relationships, partners and having children but it has never happened with me. I am certainly not going to blame having KS for me being single but it certainly has not helped. I think I was fairly normal growing up as a child but it was in my teenage years that things changed (or did not change). As people grew up into more mature activities and parties I found myself more and more socially isolated. I do not think I ever made an active decision not to participate but I found myself making up excuses not to have to go places or attend parties. Eventually people stopped asking. I do not think I was un-happy as teenager, I just was not a normal hormone driven teenager. Growing up just before the internet age perhaps made a difference. I had only a vague knowledge of what puberty and sex were. I just assumed I was one of the later developers, as the doctors told me and it would all start growing one day. I remember one day finding pages of a hard core porn magazine one day (I am that old...) I was both shocked and perhaps excited to see the men in the photos even though I looked nothing like them at the time. I was basically asexual all through my teenage and University years. I know I liked to see other men naked if I ever got the chance in a changing room but it was just curiousity at the time, there was no sexual interest. Getting diagnosed and starting treatment at the age of 23 certainly changed things but it took a while even then for any sexual feelings to develop. I was still a very slow starter with very little social and sexual confidence. It was not until my early 30's that I even tried to loose my virginity and that did not go well. I have perhaps only met two women who I have ever felt very comfortable around and they showed an interest in me. Unfortunately both times it was either before diagnosis or just after so I was in no position to notice any opportunity or perhaps even act on it. I am still in contact with both of them on social media even now but nothing developed at the time. I am now more sexually confident but still no where near as active as I would like to be. I am so used to living on my own and needing my own space I do not see myself being able to live with somebody but on the other hand I do like the odd encounter I do have and wish it could be more often. Over the years I have used Grindr occassionally and visited gay saunas, which have on the most part been fun but still isolated incidents. I do enjoy talking to fellow patients about all topics and sometimes these discussions can get iinimate. I am very open about my thoughts and experiences and happy to share them with others if they want to talk. It is sometimes frustating to have a high libido but not have a suitable outlet. I do watch porn, but not too often as it is no substitute for real intimate contact. That is more than enough text for one go. Thank you if you have made it this far, I just wanted to write a few things down. Best wishes.
